subject: 💵 Amazon's cash-flow crater
body_html:
Plus: Reddit behind the curtain | Thursday, October 29, 2026

Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Oct 29, 2026

Thursday ✅.

Today's newsletter is 858 words, a 3-minute read.

📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 0.3%.

  • ‼️ Stunning stat: Google parent Alphabet shed half a trillion in market value following yesterday's earnings.

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Crocs (+25.5%) soared on record Q3 revenue driven by international demand for its namesake foam clogs and a surprise rebound in its HeyDude slip-on business. The results, combined with a strong showing from Adidas, breathed new life into other footwear-linked stocks, including Dick's Sporting Goods (+4.3%) and Nike (+3.45%).
 
 
1 big thing: Cash-flow crater
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

It's as if Amazon said: Google, hold my beer.

  • Amazon shares fell sharply in extended trading after it reported plummeting free cash flow tied to its heavy investments in AI.

💸 Zoom in: Free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion over the 12 months ended Sept. 30, compared with a positive $14.8 billion for the same time period a year ago.

  • The company attributed the swing primarily to a $94.8 billion increase in purchases of property and equipment connected to its AI investments.
  • It expects 2026 cash capital expenditures of $220 billion.

🔍 The big picture: Investors are scrutinizing the heavy costs of AI infrastructure investments — a microscope that also dragged down Alphabet shares today after the Google parent's earnings report last night.

📉 Amazon shares are down around 6% in extended trading after already closing the day down 4.3%.

  • Alphabet finished down 12.3%.

Zoom out: Another data point from Amazon's earnings that might've unnerved investors was the 12% growth in advertising, compared with the same period a year earlier.

  • That trailed the previous quarter's 26% year-over-year growth.
  • The company's ad business could come under pressure as consumers turn to AI agents to help shop for them, though Amazon recently blocked Meta's popular Muse agent from its platform.
  • "Muse traction will likely drive questions on Amazon's agentic strategy," Bank of America analyst Justin Post wrote this week in a research note.

2. Reddit ducks behind the curtain
 

Illustration: Annelise Capossela/Axios
 

Reddit is saying goodbye to the open web and moving primarily to a log-in model, saying it no longer wants its content subject to the prying eyes of AI web scrapers.

  • Co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman told Axios' Sara Fischer today that the company is making the change to improve its user experience, bolster its ads business and prevent bots from scraping its proprietary data.
  • He expressed confidence that the change would ultimately improve engagement and monetization, even as changes to traditional search continue to impact user growth in the U.S, Sara writes.

What's next: Reddit will begin testing the fully logged-in experience this quarter outside the U.S. and collect data on the best approach before it rolls out broader changes gradually.

  • The company is still working through what content will be available to users who do not log in. Participation features, such as commenting and content ranking, will continue to be accessible only to logged-in users.

The big picture: The change was announced alongside Reddit's Q3 earnings results, which saw the ads business grow a whopping 54% year over year.

3. Other happenings
 

Photo Illustration: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
 

📉 Intel shares are plunging over 19% in extended trading following a ho-hum fourth-quarter forecast, with the company pointing to ongoing softness in the global PC market. (CNBC)

🥃 Bottoms up, bottoming out: The share of U.S. household budgets spent on alcohol fell to a record low last year, to 0.77% of average expenditures, per labor bureau data. (Bloomberg)

💉 Eli Lilly shares hit a record high after it reported surging sales of GLP-1 drugs. (MarketWatch)

⚖️ Antitrust watch: DoorDash is framing its $17 billion Instacart acquisition as a way to help smaller businesses fend off Amazon and Walmart. (Axios)

4. 🏍️ Barely a LiveWire
 

A LiveWire S2 Alpinista electric motorcycle. Photo: Courtesy of LiveWire
 

LiveWire, the electric motorcycle maker spun off from Harley-Davidson, is hanging on by a drive belt.

  • Shares skidded 43.7% today to under $1 after the company warned it may not survive the next year.

🪫 The big picture: The company — spun off from Harley in 2022 with visions of pioneering the future of motorcycling — is burning cash and selling few bikes.

  • It sold 241 electric motorcycles in the September quarter, generating just $2.7 million in revenue.
  • It generated almost twice as much in sales selling electric balance bikes and bicycles.
  • Altogether, the company posted an $18.6 million net loss for the quarter on $7.9 million of revenue, and ended September with $40 million in cash — less than half of what it had at the start of the year.

🗣️ What's next: LiveWire said it "continues to evaluate and pursue comprehensive financing and other strategic alternatives, which may include significant capital raises, strategic partnerships or investments, sales, and other strategic transactions."

🗓️ On this day in 1964, three men — Jack "Murph the Surf" Murphy, Allan Kuhn and Roger Clark — pulled off one of the biggest jewel heists in American history. Sneaking through a window at New York's American Museum of Natural History, they lifted 24 gems said to be valued over $400,000 (about $4.3 million today). Ten were eventually recovered, one was ransomed back for $25,000, and the rest were never found. None had been insured.
